items: Expecting a revert of an old commit to restore the file "as it was". Root cause: a revert merges the inverse change into today's files, with the reverted commit as base, so later edits to the same lines conflict.
Typing git revert -m "reason" <commit>. Root cause: on git revert, -m is the mainline parent number for reverting a merge, not a message.
Thinking a range revert is atomic. Root cause: a range produces one revert commit per original, newest first, so a stop at step two leaves step one committed.

Using --quit to back out of a stopped sequence. Root cause: --quit forgets the sequence but keeps the reverts already made and leaves the conflict in the index and the files; --abort is the one that returns the branch.
Reverting with staged changes. Root cause: the index must match HEAD before a revert starts.

beats.text: A change that raised a batch size was merged, deployed by CI, the team's automated pipeline, and now exhausts memory on the feature workers. Three teammates have pulled it. The CTO wants to know what exactly you run, and what nobody must run.

beats.text: Nobody must run a reset followed by a forced push. The last two videos explained why: three clones still name that commit. What you run is one command that needs no force, takes the same route as any other commit, and reaches every clone as a normal update. And when you understand what that command computes, you can also explain the day it stops with a conflict. Hold on to that day. It arrives in step five.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. This is the undo for shared history, the commits other people already have. In the map from two videos ago, the deciding question was private or shared, and the answer "shared" led to one rule: correct by adding. git revert is that rule as a command.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. This is the undo for shared history, the commits other people already have. In the map from two videos ago, the deciding question was private or shared, and the answer "shared" led to one rule: correct by adding. `git revert` is that rule as a command.

beats.text: Six things today. What a revert is: a three-way merge with unusual inputs. What it writes inside .git. Three refusals that surprise people. How to revert a range, and how to pack several reverts into one commit. Why a revert of an old commit can conflict, with the three index stages as proof. And what to do when a sequence of reverts stops halfway.

And what to do when a sequence of reverts stops halfway.

beats.text: In one sentence: git revert <commit> 🟡 CAUTION adds a commit whose change is the opposite of what <commit> changed, and removes nothing.
beats.tele: In one sentence: `git revert <commit>` 🟡 CAUTION adds a commit whose change is the opposite of what `<commit>` changed, and removes nothing.

beats.text: Why does it exist? Because a branch that other people have can only move forward without hurting them. A revert moves it forward.
beats.tele: Why does it exist? Because a branch that other people have can only move forward without hurting them. A revert moves it forward.

beats.text: Precisely. A revert is a three-way merge, the same machinery as in the merge module, with unusual inputs. A three-way merge combines two versions against a common base. Here the base is the commit being reverted: on screen, say d51208b. "Ours" is HEAD, 73572b2. "Theirs" is the parent of the reverted commit, a49e359.
beats.tele: Precisely. A revert is a three-way merge, the same machinery as in the merge module, with unusual inputs. A three-way merge combines two versions against a common base. Here the base is the commit being reverted: on screen, say `d51208b`. "Ours" is HEAD, `73572b2`. "Theirs" is the parent of the reverted commit, `a49e359`.

beats.text: Think it through with the rule table from the merge module. Between base and theirs, the difference is the reverted commit's change, read backwards. Between base and ours, the difference is everything that has happened since. The merge applies the backwards change to the current files, wherever the lines it touches are still as that commit left them.

beats.text: Three consequences follow. Any commit in the history can be reverted, not only the last. A revert can conflict. And the result is an ordinary commit on top of HEAD, so the branch only moves forward.
beats.tele: Three consequences follow. Any commit in the history can be reverted, not only the last. A revert can conflict. And the result is an ordinary commit on top of HEAD, so the branch only moves forward.

beats.text: Inside .git: one new commit, with the previous HEAD commit as its only parent and a generated message. The reflog, Git's local list of where each ref has been, gets a line that starts with revert:. ORIG_HEAD isn't written. While a revert is stopped at a conflict, REVERT_HEAD names the commit being reverted, and .git/sequencer/ holds the steps still to do.

While a revert is stopped at a conflict, `REVERT_HEAD` names the commit being reverted, and `.git/sequencer/` holds the steps still to do.

beats.text: When not to use it? On private history, where you would rather the mistake never appeared. There a reset or an amend is cleaner. And be aware of what a revert isn't: it reverses one commit, not everything since.
beats.tele: When not to use it? On private history, where you would rather the mistake never appeared. There a reset or an amend is cleaner. And be aware of what a revert isn't: it reverses one commit, not everything since.

beats.text: A picture helps. The textbook's analogy: a reversing entry in a ledger. A posted entry is never erased. A second entry with the opposite sign is posted, and both stay visible.
beats.tele: A picture helps. The textbook's analogy: a reversing entry in a ledger. A posted entry is never erased. A second entry with the opposite sign is posted, and both stay visible.

beats.text: It breaks in two places. A ledger reversal always nets to zero, while a revert is computed against the files as they're now, so later changes to the same lines produce a conflict. And a revert reverses one commit, not everything since.
beats.tele: It breaks in two places. A ledger reversal always nets to zero, while a revert is computed against the files as they're now, so later changes to the same lines produce a conflict. And a revert reverses one commit, not everything since.

beats.text: The first break is the important one. A revert isn't "go back to how it was before that commit". It is "apply the opposite of that commit's change to today's files". If today's files have moved on in the same lines, Git has two candidates and no way to choose.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Expecting a revert of an old commit to restore the file "as it was". Root cause: a revert merges the inverse change into today's files, with the reverted commit as base, so later edits to the same lines conflict.
beats.tele: Expecting a revert of an old commit to restore the file "as it was". Root cause: a revert merges the inverse change into today's files, with the reverted commit as base, so later edits to the same lines conflict.

beats.text: Typing git revert -m "reason" <commit>. Root cause: on git revert, -m is the mainline parent number for reverting a merge, not a message.
beats.tele: Typing `git revert -m "reason" <commit>`. Root cause: on `git revert`, `-m` is the mainline parent number for reverting a merge, not a message.

beats.text: Thinking a range revert is atomic. Root cause: a range produces one revert commit per original, newest first, so a stop at step two leaves step one committed.
beats.tele: Thinking a range revert is atomic. Root cause: a range produces one revert commit per original, newest first, so a stop at step two leaves step one committed.

beats.text: Using --quit to back out of a stopped sequence. Root cause: --quit forgets the sequence but keeps the reverts already made and leaves the conflict in the index and the files; --abort is the one that returns the branch.
beats.tele: Using `--quit` to back out of a stopped sequence. Root cause: `--quit` forgets the sequence but keeps the reverts already made and leaves the conflict in the index and the files; `--abort` is the one that returns the branch.

beats.text: That last point is where teams save themselves a second incident. A generated message says which commit was reverted. It doesn't say that the workers ran out of memory at batch size 64, or under which conditions the change could come back. Six weeks later someone will want to raise the batch size again. The revert commit is where they'll look.
